problem: VLFM achieves strong zero-shot ObjectNav but relies on heavy models (BLIP-2, YOLOv7-E6E, optionally GroundingDINO) that need lots of VRAM, making deployment on resource-limited hardware hard.
motivation: Real-world robots and budget workstations have limited GPU memory, so a zero-shot ObjectNav pipeline must be lightweight. The authors study which VLM, detector and VQA module combinations keep success rate while cutting VRAM, on a 12GB RTX 3060.
key_idea: Replace VLFM's BLIP-2 with CLIP-ViT-B/32 and YOLOv7-E6E with YOLOv7-W6 (optionally adding a nanoLLaVA VQA check on segmentation), cutting VRAM about 2.3x with slightly higher SR.
insight: Lighter modules are faster per step but less accurate detection and embeddings increase steps per episode (BLIP-2 141 vs 179-209 steps), so total runtime and SPL can get worse (Table 3). The nanoLLaVA VQA module helped on val-mini (SR 53.33 to 70) but hurt on the full validation split (SR 53.35 vs 54.05, SPL 27.24 vs 29.42), so small-subset gains did not generalize.
method: VLM swap: replace BLIP-2 with CLIP-ViT-B/32 (open-clip, Laion2b) as the text-image encoder for cosine similarity used in the value map (151.3M params, 806 MiB).
Detector swap: replace YOLOv7-E6E with the lighter YOLOv7-W6 (70.4M, 1482 MiB) and drop GroundingDINO, restricting to COCO classes.
Segmentation: keep MobileSAM to extract object contour; the nearest depth point in the contour is the goal waypoint.
Optional VQA: nanoLLaVA (1.1B) checks whether the detected contour is visually correct; it is not used as a VLM because it lacks text embeddings.
Policy: keep VLFM's pretrained PointNav RL policy (VER-trained, depth-based), with frontier and value maps producing waypoints.

setting.backbone: CLIP-ViT-B/32 + YOLOv7-W6 + MobileSAM (+ optional nanoLLaVA), pretrained frozen; pretrained PointNav policy
setting.training_data: none (zero-shot; reuses pretrained checkpoints and VLFM's PointNav policy)
setting.action_space: waypoints executed by a pretrained PointNav policy (low-level discrete actions)

numbers_note: Split for val-mini is listed as val (subset of HM3D validation). VLFM baseline on the full val split is quoted as 30.4 SPL / 52.5 SR, from the paper's comparison table.
results: On 2000 HM3D val episodes, CLIP+YOLOv7-W6 gets SR 54.05 and SPL 29.42 vs VLFM (BLIP-2) SR 52.5 / SPL 30.4, with about 2.3x less VRAM. It beats PIRLNav in SPL (27.1) but not SR (64.1), and beats ZSON and ESC on both.
limitations: Only evaluated in simulation on HM3D, not on real robots or MP3D/Gibson.
RL policy not retrained; the VQA module gives no benefit at scale and nanoLLaVA cannot serve as the VLM.
Lighter models increase steps per episode, lowering SPL and sometimes lengthening runtime; the Table 5 VLFM comparison also mixes reported and reproduced numbers.
